title: Maya, the passing pull
hook: the pull of the passing world, attractive and fleeting, is called maya

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five virtues: truth, contentment, compassion, humility and love; your line was five guards at the door. Today, the pull those guards are guarding against.

You open your phone to check the weather. Forty minutes later you're watching a stranger restore a rusty knife, and you've added a jacket to a cart. Nothing bad happened. Everything was pretty: the knife shiny, the jacket soft, the video calming. And none of it is what you meant to do with those forty minutes. It's a familiar pull: bright, sweet, and gone the moment you look away. The Gurus had a word for it, long before phones: maya.
screen: `CHECK THE WEATHER.` → `FORTY MINUTES LATER.` → `ALL OF IT PRETTY.` → `MAYA.`

segments.voice: Maya is an old Indian word, and different traditions use it differently. In some Hindu schools it can mean the world as a kind of illusion. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the stress falls somewhere else. In the Granth's telling, the world is real; the Creator made it and lives in it. Maya is the pull of its passing parts: money, status, comfort, attachment, anything bright that promises to last and doesn't. The problem isn't that things are fake. It's that people lean their whole weight on things that were only ever passing through. The Granth gives maya many pictures. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, has a short salok near the very end of the book: as a bubble rises on water and vanishes, he says, so the world is made; Nanak says, listen, friend. The bubble is real. It even has a rainbow on it. It just isn't a place to live. Another hymn calls maya a snake that has wrapped itself around the world. And notice what Sikh teaching does not say: run to the forest, give up your job, leave your family. The Gurus taught a householder's path: work, family, and the Name. The ideal is to live in the middle of the bright, busy world and not be owned by it, like a lotus that grows in water and stays dry. That's the question maya asks on an ordinary afternoon: am I using this, or is it using me? Pretty isn't the enemy. Forgetting that it's passing is.
screen: `AN OLD WORD, USED MANY WAYS.` · `NOT FAKE — JUST PASSING.` · `A BUBBLE ON WATER.` · `IN THE WORLD, NOT OWNED BY IT.` · then, large: `PRETTY, AND PASSING.`

segments.voice: Think of one pull that got you today, a screen, a purchase, a worry about how you look, a craving, and picture it clearly, the way it shines, without scolding yourself. Now see it as a bubble on water, catching the light, and say quietly: pretty, and passing. Then let your attention come back to the breath, which is also passing, and also here.
Maya. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the pull of the passing world: bright, attractive, and gone. Not a lie, just not a home.
Your line: pretty, and passing. A bubble on water: real, bright, and not a place to live. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of maya as the pull of wealth, status and attachment; the Gurus taught living as householders in the world, working and raising families, while remembering the Name so as not to be ruled by that pull.

original.note: Gurmukhi: maya, the pull of the passing world; in Gurbani it's often spelled and sung with three syllables.

trapdoor: what you thought: maya means everything is an illusion.
what it means: in Sikh teaching, the world is real, and maya is the pull of its passing things when we lean on them as if they lasted.
what a scholar hears: an old Sanskrit word with different meanings across Indian schools; the Granth often pictures it through images like a bubble and a snake, and pairs it with attachment (moh).

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427 (Salok Mahala 9: the bubble on water)

notes: The bubble salok (jaise jal te budbudaa upjai binsai neet) is cited to Ang 1427, Salok Mahala 9; confirm the Ang and salok number.
The snake image (maya hoee naaganee jagat rahee lapattaae) is cited to Ang 510, Gujri ki Var, salok Mahala 3; confirm.

Editor review: the narrator no longer states 'the world is real; the Creator made it' as fact but as the Granth's telling; cut the moving-shade image (no reference found) from the teach, match and trapdoor; 'the Gurus were householders' became 'the Gurus taught a householder's path' (Guru Har Krishan died as a child); hook no longer says 'everybody knows this pull'.
The lotus-in-water image is cited to Sidh Gosht (Ang 938); confirm the Ang.
The contrast with 'some Hindu schools' (maya as illusion, e.g. Advaita Vedanta) is stated briefly and without ranking; confirm the wording is fair to both.
